children: Wheat for December delivery fell 0.7% to $7.25 3/4 a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade Thursday, as exports from elsewhere in the world appear to be taking up some of the space left unfulfilled by the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
Corn for December delivery fell 0.6% to $5.31 a bushel.
Soybeans for November fell 0.1% to $13.19 1/2 a bushel.

Eyes Overseas: Russian wheat exports are much lower compared with previous months and weeks due to the conflict with Ukraine affecting Black Sea shipments. However, that slowdown is having a lesser effect on wheat supply globally than anticipated. "We still have too much wheat in the United States and cheaper alternative sources are currently filling the void to this point," StoneX's Arlan Suderman said in a note.

Making More Cuts: U.S. corn fields appear to be showing yields that are even less than the cuts seen in September's WASDE report. "Early yield data has [us] wondering whether NASS [National Agricultural Statistics Service] will cut its U.S. corn yield forecast by another 2-3 [bushels per acre] in October," said AgResource in a note, adding that early harvest returns are showing "disappointing" results. In the September report, the USDA projected the average corn yield at 178.5 bushels an acre--a forecast that may be even lower next month.

Next Big Thing: Traders are turning their focus to meetings between the U.S. and China heading into next week. "The next big input will be the Sunday meeting between Treasury Secretary Bessent and Chinese Economy Minister He," Marex's Charlie Sernatinger said in a note. "Then the big enchilada is the Thursday meeting between Xi and Trump." The grain markets hold out hope for clarity on future Chinese demand for U.S. grains, but futures were bogged down after Wednesday's interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve.

Cost of Doing Business: The supply of soymeal--soybeans ground up for use in products such as food or for processing into soybean oil--appears to be tight as users of soymeal struggle to buy the supply they need. "Basis levels around the Midwest are strengthening as the rainfall is slowing harvest and limiting the amount of product that is flowing to the processors," said Brian Hoops of Midwest Market Solutions.

World Wide: Higher fuel prices and costs for other inputs like fertilizer may weigh on farmers during the next planting season in South America. "Crude oil is easing off but still at painfully high levels for all corners of the globe as this will surely cause issues in South American planting from fertilizer to acres planted," Futures International's Gary Sandlund said in a note. Planting in South America typically begins in September and continues to the end of the year.

Now and Later: Prices for diesel look to wreak havoc on farmer's budgets during the U.S. harvesting season next year, the American Farm Bureau Federation said in a note. "Diesel prices are on the rise as harvest begins across the country, adding another cost for farmers during one of the most fuel-intensive times of the year," Faith Parum of the AFBF said in a note. The average price of diesel per gallon is nearly $6.40 a gallon, AAA said Thursday, which is an all-time record. On-farm diesel prices are nearly double of where they were last year, Parum said, quoting them at $5.45 a gallon. "Margins are already thin, and farmers are facing record-high production costs," she said.
The USDA will release its monthly Cattle on Feed report at 3 p.m. ET Friday.
The CFTC will release its weekly Commitment of Traders report at 3:30 p.m. ET Friday.
The USDA will release its weekly Grain Export Inspections report at 11 a.m. ET Monday.
The USDA will release its weekly Crop Progress report at 4 p.m. ET Monday.
